We envision a different dynamic: in a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates evidence that stimulates further investigations. Such chains of information collision and empirical validation could transform isolated discovery loops into a cumulative scientific process. We propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint for enabling these evidence-driven chain reactions. ESI preserves experimental records in shared, computable scientific memory, where evidence from different domains can be recombined into testable hypotheses. It jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, then coordinates physical tests across distributed experimental nodes. Their feedback revises hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build the infrastructure for scientific intelligence that evolves through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.
title: Evolving Scientific Intelligence: From Fragmented Evidence to Distributed Experimental Loops

abstract: Attention is the computational core of large language models, yet the verifiers that bound how far an attention head's output can move under input perturbations give no guarantee on how loose their bounds are. A weak certificate therefore cannot be told apart from a fragile model. We develop a conic programming theory of attention certification that supplies this guarantee. We prove that the difficulty lies not in the softmax but in the bilinear interaction of a varying query with the keys. This interaction makes certification NP-hard over boxes and inapproximable once the attention logits can move by a constant amount. A fixed query or listed token substitutions, by contrast, make the exact worst case efficiently computable. An exponential cone moment relaxation then certifies a head with an error bounded quadratically in the perturbation radius by computable quantities, an order that cannot be improved. We also show that relaxations that treat a network one operation at a time, linear bound propagation among them, pay on second-order terms a sum of per-operation maxima instead of one coupled maximum. Computational results on GPT-2 indicate that the theory carries over to a trained model. Against exact worst cases with the query fixed, the certificate attains the predicted second-order accuracy. It is tighter than linear bound propagation on every head, and the looseness of bound propagation tracks the predicted per-operation excess.
title: Conic Certification of Transformer Attention

abstract: Recently, reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is practically very important, where the leading approach is group relative policy optimization (GRPO) that typically faces a trade-off between rollout efficiency and downstream performance. To improve efficiency while preserving performance, existing selective rollout methods mainly exploit only source-side training dynamics to optimize the discrete distribution over source prompts. However, in practice, the source training dataset is rarely identically distributed to the target test dataset. When such a mismatch exists, due to legal or privacy constraints, it is usually not acceptable to share target prompts themselves with the RLVR trainer. Nevertheless, it is still possible for the target data owner to provide limited aggregated feedback from a small held-out target set without revealing target prompts or rollout traces. In this paper, we propose learning-to-reweight rollout (L2RR) that explicitly incorporates target-side performance feedback into GRPO. Specifically, L2RR learns a discrete sampling distribution over source prompts by optimizing a bi-level objective that maximizes accuracy on a held-out target dataset, while simultaneously penalizing rollouts that provide little incremental learning information. Empirical studies on six math reasoning benchmarks and three model scales show that L2RR improves target-domain performance and increases rollout efficiency.
title: Dataset Mismatch Matters in Group Relative Policy Optimization for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards

abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference with a drafter whose proposed tokens are verified by the target model in parallel. Under lossless speculative sampling, a draft token is accepted with probability one minus the total variation (TV) distance between the target and draft distributions, yet drafters are often trained with cross-entropy (CE) or KL. We first show that under matched and well-tuned training, TV matches or surpasses several published draft-training objectives when fine-tuning, and a fixed TV and KL mixture does the same when training from scratch. We identify two remaining problems, TV's vanishing gradients on undercovered tokens and the prefix products that starve later positions in acceptance-length objectives. To address both, we derive TVP, a loss family based on expected acceptance length, whose power parameter interpolates between coverage and acceptance oriented objectives. Annealing the power from zero to one gives the highest or tied-highest acceptance length across three drafter architectures and three target models, including longer drafts and block verification. TVP improves acceptance length over CE by 9.8% when fine-tuning, and over the public DFlash2 training recipes by 6.2 to 12.9%.
title: TVP: TV is Almost All You Need for Speculative Decoding

abstract: Adam keeps two FP32 moments per parameter, twice the bytes of the FP32 weights, yet compressing them is risky: the update divides by the square root of the second moment, so small reconstruction errors can change the restored computation substantially. We study guarded moment compression, in which a coordinate's decoded moments are accepted only if they reproduce the native FP32 Adam update to within a tolerance $τ$, in units of the learning rate, for every gradient in a clipped domain; all other coordinates are stored exactly. The natural certificate, which ranges each update separately over gradient intervals, fails: on one million trained OPT-125M coordinates it escapes 98.9% of coordinates and the payload grows to 126.6% of raw FP32. Our key observation is that both updates consume the same gradient and parameter. Bounding their difference directly, with FP32 rounding-error allowances and a fixed mixed linear-logarithmic gradient partition, cuts escapes to 0.53% and the payload to 28.3% at $τ=0.01$. Across 120 complete-checkpoint restores of OPT-125M and ResNet-18, with four trained seeds and three training fractions per model, guarded 8-bit log codes shrink moment payloads by 69.5% and 71.9% relative to FP32, 40.8% and 45.4% relative to equally guarded BF16, and 29.3% and 37.6% relative to equally guarded blockwise 8-bit, and every restored first update stays within tolerance. Encoding and restoration together take 2.3-2.6$\times$ as long as guarded BF16 but less time than guarded blockwise 8-bit. Searching both moment codes jointly saves under 0.001% more bytes at 6% more codec time, so per-moment rounding suffices. The guarantee covers the first restored update under a pinned Torch operation model; we measure subsequent training empirically.
title: Guarded Compression of Adam Optimizer State with Shared-Gradient Bounds

abstract: Activation recomputation saves accelerator memory by replaying forward segments during the backward pass, but replay is only correct if it sees the state the original forward pass saw. Mutable buffers, aliased bytes and random-generator state can change in between, so re-executing unchanged code can differentiate a different computation. We make this state explicit. A versioned replay contract specifies what replay must restore, and a joint planner chooses, per segment, between activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots and selective-region preservation, charging each option its measured memory and recovery cost. Independent derivative and byte-level checks validate the contract, and a Torch/JAX cohort retains all 5,900 execution records, including matches, rejections and divergences. On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, each measured over fifty fresh processes, joint planning reduces paired step time by 18.16% against a correctly costed eager/whole planner at a 44 GiB budget (approximate 97.5% ratio interval $[.8172,.8195]$). At 32 GiB, where the eager/whole planner has no feasible static policy, joint planning is 4.98% faster than fixed regions at 29.94 rather than 26.20 GiB. A complete CIFAR-100 dense-queue application runs seven methods for 100 encoder and 25 probe epochs at six training seeds, with byte-identical test scores within each seed. There, joint planning uses 22.41% more allocated memory than whole snapshots, with a process-time geometric-mean ratio of 1.0080 (seed range $[.9845,1.0191]$). Together, the results map where selective preservation pays off: sparse writes with large activations benefit, while in the dense-queue workload whole snapshots use less allocated memory.
title: State-Aware Activation Recomputation with Replay Contracts and Selective Preservation

abstract: Finding the passage that answers a question is the first step of most practical systems built on documents, and for Tajik we found no openly described model for it. We present Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large, a Tajik text embedder built from multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters). We asked our own Tajik language model to write questions for passages from Tajik laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text, and trained on 235,140 question and passage pairs for one epoch, with hard negatives chosen by another embedder and English and Russian pairs mixed in so the model would not forget those languages. On laws the model had never seen, the right passage is among the top ten results for 93.6% of questions, up from 80.2%; on tax documents, 94.5% against 82.6%. On Belebele, the one test we have that was written by people, the gain is smaller and not confirmed (92.2% to 95.2%, with touching intervals), and Russian and English do not change. On law and tax questions written in the same style as its training questions, it is tied with Giga-Embeddings-3B, a model five times its size; on Belebele the 3B and 8B models score slightly higher, and only after we fine-tuned them on our data are they clearly ahead. We also report what failed: training in bfloat16 broke the model, and replacing Tajik letters with similar Russian ones did not help. Our law, tax and Wikipedia test questions come from the same model that wrote the training questions, so we treat those scores as an upper limit until questions written by Tajik speakers are available.
title: Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large: Fine-Tuning a 560M Embedder for Tajik Retrieval

abstract: A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every $d$ rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size $d$ is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no $d>1$ used throughout the network reliably outperforms $d=1$, and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At $d=1$, the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.
title: Do Orthogonality Constraints Help Language-Model Training Beyond Sphere Optimization?

abstract: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents \emph{X-World~1.6}, advancing X-World~1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
title: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models

abstract: Does eliciting five weighted estimates within a single response change how a language model responds to information? Across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction, and status-quo/default tasks, we compare direct numerical answers with a multi-estimate response format, contrasting source framings, explicitly random cues, and probability-consistency constraints. We evaluate three completed configurations--gpt-6.1-sol, claude-sonnet-5.5, and Qwen3-8B (reasoning disabled, analyzed descriptively). In the first two configurations, direct elicitation yielded near-zero irrelevant-anchor indices and status-quo effects, while remaining responsive to informative sources and informed advice. Of 23 preregistered confirmatory tests, six rejected after Holm adjustment; however, all six absolute point estimates fell below their prespecified smallest effect sizes of interest without establishing equivalence. Moreover, while separate versus joint elicitation shifted conjunction judgments, interpretation is constrained by between-call noise. Ultimately, multi-estimate elicitation failed to produce uniform debiasing or response attenuation across tasks and models, though post hoc correlations between candidate spread and anchoring error motivate independent predictive validation. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies
title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments

abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $π_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit https://doubleblind-sae-pi05.github.io for video rollouts.
title: Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$

abstract: Conversational text-to-SQL interfaces could give healthcare professionals natural-language access to electronic health record (EHR) data, but evidence for their real-world usability remains limited: prior evaluations have relied largely on curated benchmarks with fully specified questions or on simulated users. We report a user study in which 14 physicians who regularly work with EHR data used both a single-turn and a conversational multi-turn text-to-SQL interface over the MIMIC-IV database in a within-subjects design; dialogue analyses additionally drew on interaction logs from 21 healthcare professionals across the main study and two pilot studies. The conversational interface was consistently favored: mean System Usability Scale scores rose from 68.2, near the industry average, to 85.9 (p<0.001), with significant advantages across technology-acceptance constructs including performance expectancy, effort expectancy, self-efficacy, and behavioral intention. In post-study forced-choice comparisons, 93% of participants reported greater overall satisfaction with the conversational interface, 86% preferred it for real-world adoption, and 71% trusted its results more; no participant preferred or trusted the single-turn interface more. Turn-level analysis of 425 logged user turns showed that freely composed queries triggered clarification requests in 24.8% of cases versus 1.8% for predefined, fully specified questions, and 64.3% of clarification episodes stemmed from EHR- or clinical-domain knowledge. Conversational interaction is a practical prerequisite, rather than a convenience, for natural-language EHR access. The frequent need for clarification in realistic clinical queries further underscores the importance of conversational interfaces, while benchmark-style evaluation can substantially underrepresent the ambiguity of real clinical use.
title: Conversational Interaction for LLM-Based Clinical Text-to-SQL: A User Study with Healthcare Professionals

abstract: Attribution graphs over the features of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to predict what an ablation does and are compared across training seeds. A TopK SAE keeps the largest preactivations at each token, and a feature's margin is its preactivation's distance to the cutoff. On five public TopK SAE pairs from three Pythia models, zeroing one feature moves a next layer feature across the cutoff in 0.74 of cases or more, and the crossings carry most of the response's energy. Over writes that scale a feature's code by three factors, the graph built on the features active beforehand has a median relative error of 0.247 or more. The margin graph adds the first order change to every preactivation and reranks, at the same cost, and errs by at most 0.033. At the median, the crossing features' decoded change is 1.24 times the model's own change in norm or more. Between seeds of one testbed, sparse maps between features explain 0.85 of a graph's energy on its active features, and 0.47 once the other seed's graph keeps only its own. The largest model studied is pythia-160m.
title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin

abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) unlearning is often treated as an objective-design problem: given multimodal forget data, the goal is to optimize a loss that removes undesirable behavior while preserving retained capabilities. We argue that this view overlooks an equally important data-centric question: how should each forget example be represented before optimization? Existing methods typically keep image-conditioned failures in their original image-text form, implicitly assuming that pixels are the right route for unlearning whenever pixels appear in the input. We challenge this assumption by constructing modality-decomposed versions of VLM benchmarks, enabling controlled comparisons among image-only, text-only, and multimodal representations of the same examples. Our modality-mixing experiments show that unsafe instruction-following behavior is more effectively suppressed through textual representations than through images alone, while purely text-only unlearning can still weaken visual grounding when the target behavior depends on visual evidence. Motivated by this trade-off, we introduce ModRoute, a gradient-guided per-sample modality routing strategy that selectively converts high visual-pressure examples to text-only form while keeping the remaining examples multimodal. Notably, on VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, ModRoute has the strongest composite unlearning-utility score of 0.847 at $γ=0.5$, a 2.5% improvement over the best random-switching score and $\geq$46% better than pure multimodal or text unlearning. Overall, our results show that effective VLM unlearning depends not only on the objective, but also on the composition and per-sample modality routing of the unlearning data.
title: Words Before Pixels: Selective Modality Routing for Vision-Language Model Unlearning

abstract: Natural-language driven smart home control remains challenging: cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) raise privacy concerns, while local Small Language Models (SLMs) can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests. We introduce Trail (Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes), a fully local framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions. Trail exploits the natural structure of a home's action space, selecting a room, device, and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry. This ensures valid actions while enabling confidence-based abstention when requests cannot be reliably resolved. We also design a structured memory module that uses typed decisions to support user preferences, device references, and multi-turn interactions. To evaluate Trail, we extend HomeBench and generate three datasets: Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variation; Trek-Robust, which evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description; and Trek-Memory, which assesses conversational memory across multi-turn interactions. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the requests that depend on earlier turns, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.
title: Trail: Accurate Local Smart Home Control Using Decision Models

abstract: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents

abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) may contain physiological information related to hereditary cancer susceptibility, but its relationship with future cancer risk remains unclear. Here, we present ECG2Gene, a two-stage deep-learning framework that derives digital phenotypes related to germline tumor susceptibility from routine 12-lead ECGs and predicts future cancer risk. In Stage 1, carrier status for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in ATM, BRIP1, CHEK2, PALB2, BRCA1, and BRCA2 supervises a multitask model that generates six continuous ECG-derived gene scores. In Stage 2, XGBoost integrates these scores with clinical variables to predict subsequent breast and ovarian cancer in women and prostate cancer in men. We also introduce ECG-Wide Association Analysis (EWAS) to characterize associations between ECG-derived gene scores and ECG waveforms. Across the clinical feature combinations evaluated in UK Biobank, the best-performing sex-specific models achieve AUROCs of 0.683, 0.633, and 0.660 for breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer, respectively. In external evaluations, models combining ECG-derived gene scores with age achieve prostate cancer AUROCs of 0.709 and 0.579 among men in the overall China Kadoorie Biobank and MIMIC-IV-ECG cohorts, respectively. ECG2Gene links genetically supervised ECG phenotyping and waveform association analysis to future cancer outcomes, demonstrating the potential of routine ECGs combined with clinical information for non-invasive, opportunistic cancer risk assessment.
title: ECG2Gene: Deep Learning-Based Germline Tumor Susceptibility Gene Risk Assessment Using Electrocardiograms

abstract: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $π_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.
title: Learning from an Imitable Teacher: Competition Solution for the MetaFine Challenge

abstract: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.
title: Enhancing Language Model Reasoning with Structured Multi-Level Modeling

abstract: Transient thermal fields during solidification connect casting process conditions and cooling behaviour to the formation of defect-prone regions in aluminum cast ings. Repeatedly solving this thermal problem across geometries and process conditions is computationally expensive, motivating data-driven surrogate models. However, existing machine-learning studies on casting thermal behaviour rely on study-specific simulation databases that do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking. We introduce LM6-CastBench, an open simulation dataset for geometry-aware learning of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, combining three geometry families, ten variants per family, five pouring tempera tures, and three mould temperatures (450 geometry-process cases in total). Each case retains CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata, and time-resolved nodal temperatures. We benchmark a point wise MLP against a spatially structured U-Net under geometry-level data splits; the U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin, with the biggest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes. LM6-CastBench gives researchers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for geometry-aware surro gate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.
title: LM6-CastBench: A Geometry-Aware Simulation Dataset for Transient Thermal Prediction in LM6 Sand Casting

abstract: A central obstacle in realizing color center cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is inhomogeneity, or disorder, among individual emitters. As the number of emitters increases, so does the complexity of the experimental data, making it difficult to quantify the present physical mechanisms of disorder. Here we introduce an artificial intelligence-driven model discovery framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent, equipped with tools and a structured workflow, proposes candidate Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generates computational tools, and quantitatively evaluates competing physical hypotheses. We apply the workflow to three previously published experimental cavity-QED datasets collected from color centers in diamond and silicon carbide. Across the experiments, the agent successfully identifies physical models for the system and characterizes the disorder. In assessing reproducibility, we find that run-to-run variability is concentrated primarily in the research plan generation step, while the computational analysis itself is substantially more consistent. Our results suggest that structured LLM agent workflows can support model discovery from quantum optical experimental data while simultaneously allowing for human expert supervision and collaboration.
title: Discovering Models for Experimental Quantum Systems with Agentic AI

abstract: Automated configuration of mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers largely relies on black-box optimization. Each trial requires an expensive solver run and provides only a scalar outcome, so tuning can require many such evaluations. Human experts take a different approach. They inspect solver logs, identify performance bottlenecks, and adjust the parameters that address them. We propose Log-Driven Semantic Tuning (LDST), which uses a large language model (LLM) to automate this process. LDST extracts compact diagnostics from solver logs, uses the LLM to propose sparse edits to the current best configuration based on parameter meanings and observed solver behavior, and validates each proposal before execution. A regime-adaptive objective selects the tuning signal according to the information available from a time-limited run, while a log-based completion signal estimates completion time from branch-and-bound tree growth recorded in ordinary solver logs, so that solved and unsolved runs share one time scale. On 215 instances from five benchmark sets, LDST reduces geometric-mean loss by 43.9% on easy instances and 16.7% on intermediate instances relative to the best of SMAC3, RBFOpt, and random search. In both regimes, LDST achieves a lower loss with 10 proposals than any of these baselines achieves with 50. Configurations that LDST tunes on a single instance also transfer better than baseline configurations to unseen instances of the same family.
title: Log-Driven Semantic Tuning for Mixed Integer Programming Solvers

abstract: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.
title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale

abstract: Extracting knowledge from large databases of experimental materials data requires repeated analyses and reusable records of their choices and results. We developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA), a multi-agent system in which AI agents with distinct roles analyze experimental thermoelectric data under predefined instructions and quality checks, saving analysis records traceable to their sources. In four experiments varying theme and cycle counts, we measured what accumulated in these records. In the largest experiment (100 analyses across 10 themes and 10 cycles), concept co-occurrences were concentrated within themes, vocabulary was shared across themes and some relation descriptions were first detected in later cycles. A specialized AI that searches this experiment's knowledge bases and reads their analysis records answered materials questions with cited sources. Retrospective checks, including tracing an answer generated with a preliminary corpus back to the source data, exposed errors: traceability makes errors findable but not absent.
title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI

abstract: Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. We introduce Unsatz, a benchmark in which an LLM agent must construct the ansatz itself. Each task is a simulated system, generated from a private seed as a program in a small modeling language: ordinary, delay, or partial differential equations, discrete maps, static and causal models, or stochastic processes, possibly with hidden states, distorted sensors, and uninformative measurement channels. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs in the same language, obtains their coefficients from the benchmark's fitter, and is scored only on how its final program predicts experiments it never saw: conditions outside the range it could explore, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solve between 21% and 60%. On 44 of these systems, classical equation-discovery methods almost never succeed, although the same data usually suffice once the true equations are given with unknown coefficients; the difficulty lies in finding the structure, not in estimating it. Because mechanisms recur across systems, we also give agents the program they discovered for a related system; it helped only when the new system shared the mechanism and the first investigation had succeeded. Stronger agents make fewer unscientific errors; beyond these, agents find which variables a system has but not how they act, and prefer revisions that lower the training error to revisions that predict better.
title: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz

abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.
title: TopoQuant: Topological Framework to Characterize Behavioral Shifts in Quantized Large Language Models

abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,532 articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their steady-state reference efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.
title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization

abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,035 training articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.
title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization

abstract: Data-driven control in radio access networks (RANs) selects resource allocations using associations between control actions and key performance indicators (KPIs) learned from network telemetry. Because the shared radio environment influences both the scheduler's decisions and the resulting performance, a bias known as confounding, such associations overstate the effect of an allocation and misdirect resources toward user equipment (UEs) that cannot benefit. Moreover, individual UEs respond heterogeneously to the same decision, so even a corrected average effect does not identify which UEs gain from additional resources. While causal inference has recently been applied to RANs, existing approaches do not model the cross-layer mechanisms that connect an allocation to its outcome. In this paper, a hierarchical structural causal model (H-SCM) spanning the PHY, MAC, and network layers is proposed that separates cell-load confounding from UE-specific response heterogeneity. In particular, a counterfactual scheduling problem is formulated in which physical resource block (PRB) allocations are selected using per-UE counterfactual goodput rather than observational conditional averages. This problem is solved via a pipeline combining constrained causal discovery, structural-equation fitting, and abduction-action-prediction. Simulations demonstrate that naive observational estimation overstates the full-PRB response by 73.3%, whereas adjustment for cell-load confounding reduces the relative error to 9.8%. Held-out interventions are predicted with a coefficient of determination of 0.988. Counterfactual scheduling achieves a mean relative loss in total cell goodput below 0.5% against the ground-truth optimum, compared with 2.0-2.9% for a neural-network baseline.
title: From Confounding to Counterfactuals: A Cross-Layer Causal Model for RAN Scheduling

abstract: Primal-dual methods enforce safety constraints in reinforcement learning through Lagrangian relaxation. For a fixed policy, the exact bounded multiplier response exhibits bang-bang switching at the constraint boundary. Practical gradient updates can oscillate through coupling with policy optimization. We propose Structural DuaL Adaptation (SDLA), which replaces this bang-bang response with a unique continuous response through current-cost centering, trajectory weighting, and quadratic regularization. We characterize activation thresholds and response sensitivity. Ternary search computes multipliers without a dual gradient stepsize. For entropy-regularized tabular policies, we bound equilibrium constraint violations alongside reward gaps. We establish convergence of delayed updates under mild assumptions. Neural PPO/SAC experiments on OmniSafe and HASARD demonstrate competitive rewards with improved constraint tracking. On HASARD, PPO-SDLA achieves higher reported mean reward than the human baseline in six of eighteen settings while meeting the respective mean-cost budgets, including four with lower mean cost. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of higher mean reward at lower mean cost than the human baseline across multiple HASARD settings.
title: Structural Dual Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.
title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics

abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) explains a computation in a trained network by identifying the components and variables that implement it and testing them with interventions. Singular learning theory (SLT) describes the same network through the geometry of the loss around its parameters, summarized by the local learning coefficient. In pretrained language models the two have not been compared: SLT's estimates at this scale concern whole models or components whose roles were not independently established, and the estimator, which averages the loss over parameter settings drawn near the trained ones, has had no reference for how far those draws may move the parameters. We show that both are functions of one object, the map from a component's parameters to the model's predictions under inputs and interventions, whose first derivatives determine the Fisher information, the learning coefficient, and intervention effects, and whose higher derivatives add a quartic correction and pairwise terms. We test this correspondence in Pythia-1B on Dyck bracket matching at all 154 training checkpoints, against a five-stage circuit identified by interventions. We measure the local geometry of all 144 components inside the region where predictions are preserved, with the Fisher spectrum at every checkpoint, which gives the quadratic part of the learning-coefficient estimate at every temperature. Changes of the Fisher trace track changes of causal effect (median partial rank correlation 0.51), largely as a trend shared across the model, whereas the gain Fisher of a component's output and the large-temperature count are specific to the component. The count follows causal change across the population but not the growth of a formed circuit component. The quartic part is what a sampler that leaves the region registers beyond curvature. Pairwise interaction curvature tracks joint-ablation interactions.
title: Bridging Singular Learning Theory and Mechanistic Interpretability at the Billion-Parameter Scale

abstract: Distributed support vector machine (SVM) learning is challenging under heterogeneous local data and limited communication. We develop a Representative Learning framework based on Lifted Empirical Risk Minimization, replacing each covariate by a local Gaussian distribution. For linear SVMs, the resulting expected hinge loss has an exact closed form, is smooth for nondegenerate lifting covariances, and converges to the ordinary hinge loss as the covariance vanishes. The lifted formulation enables clouded representatives that encode both location and covariance. We study a model-independent Mean Representative (MR) and a Score-Matching Representative (SMR) that matches the class-wise lifted gradient at its construction parameter. We show that SMR covariance scaling is stable with respect to within-group heterogeneity and that the gradient discrepancy between full data and frozen representatives is controlled by the maximum within-group diameter. Under strong convexity and smoothness, this yields an inexact-gradient convergence guarantee. Experiments under heterogeneous class allocation show that lifted representatives remain competitive with centralized solutions, while SMR more closely recovers the centralized lifted-SVM optimizer. We further extend the framework to nonlinear SVMs through a shared kernel dictionary, with experiments on Ionosphere and Australian Credit Approval showing analogous behavior. These results provide a distributional representative framework for communication-efficient distributed SVM learning under heterogeneity.
title: Representative Learning for Distributed Support Vector Machines

abstract: LLM research-ideation systems aim for hypotheses that are both true and non-obvious, yet neither property can normally be checked. We build a testbed in which both can. Generators propose conditional interaction claims about two fully tabulated benchmarks, NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench; every claim is verified exactly against the tables, and its non-obviousness is scored against a calibrated blind prior elicited from other LLMs. Excess truth measures how much more often a run's claims hold than this panel expects. Across a series of pre-registered stages with Claude and GPT generators, our main positive result is a simple two-stage step found by a harness optimizer: draft a large pool of claims, then select a subset in a separate call. For Sonnet on NAS-Bench-201, this step raised excess truth in every pre-registered test, including against a same-pool ablation that keeps only likely-true claims, without lowering precision. The gain comes both from credit for true claims and from avoiding near-miss false ones. In post hoc checks it held under every calibration, panel and truth rule we tried, and it exceeded random and type-filter selection from the same pools. Because kept claims recur across runs, the evidence weakens when runs and claims are resampled jointly, and it is not significant against Sonnet's own prior. Two secondary findings are also pre-registered. GPT makes real use of the results of cheap probes, beating shuffled and withheld controls, though not more efficiently than asking for more claims. Optimizing the harness for an LLM judge raised judge scores while sharply cutting precision for every generator.
title: Selecting LLM-Generated Hypotheses Raises Truth Beyond What an LLM Panel Expects: A Pre-registered Study on NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench

abstract: Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.
title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design

abstract: On-device language models can learn a user's preferences through adapters trained on private data. However, a base-model upgrade may change the layers or vocabulary, leaving the personal adapter incompatible. Replacing it with a non-personal adapter loses much of the personalization, while retraining requires retaining the user's labeled history. We present Heirloom, a system that transfers a personal adapter to a new base model on the phone without retaining labels. Heirloom uses the old personal model as a teacher, collecting its predictions on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor-provided prompts, or prompts generated by the new base. It then unloads the old base and trains an adapter for the new model to match those predictions, keeping only one base model in memory at a time. We evaluate Heirloom across three generation upgrades from two model families, an architecture-preserving refresh, and three personalization tasks. On movie tagging, migration from stored inputs maintains pre-upgrade accuracy and differs from labeled retraining by at most 1.7 percentage points across the three upgrades. On a phone's neural processing unit (NPU), a fixed-length migration for the 4B upgrade takes 38 minutes and consumes 20% of the battery end to end, making the stored-input setting feasible during overnight charging.
title: Heirloom: Carrying a Phone's Personalization Across Base-Model Generations

abstract: Serving and fine-tuning a large language model on the same GPUs can turn the idle capacity between inference bursts into training progress, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes this co-location cheap because both workloads read a single frozen copy of the base weights. The difficulty lies in the fine-tuning backward pass, which has no counterpart in inference. Current co-serving systems schedule backward work per serving iteration: each iteration carries a fixed backward budget, and requests that arrive in the meantime wait for it to finish, so fine-tuning dictates inference latency whenever load spikes. We observe that the backward pass of a LoRA microbatch decomposes into per-layer tasks over the same weights that the inference forward pass visits, which allows backward work to be scheduled at layer rather than iteration granularity. Building on this observation, LayerLoom attaches same-layer backward tasks to the inference forward pass and, at each layer, runs only as many of them as the latency slack of in-flight requests permits. To keep a ready task at every layer, LayerLoom maintains a wavefront of fine-tuning microbatches staggered across layers, and it bounds the wavefront's activation memory by offloading microbatch state to host memory and prefetching it ahead of the layer where the scheduler plans to use it. A fused kernel serves the paired forward and backward GEMMs from a single read of each base weight. Because all backward work of an iteration finishes within its forward pass, new requests join the next iteration as in continuous batching. On an RTX 4090 GPU running Llama-3.1-8B under a bursty production trace, LayerLoom raises joint SLO attainment by 13.5-21.8 points over prior works with fine-tuning throughput that is comparable or up to 12% higher, and it reaches the same training losses.
title: Inference First, Training Underneath: Layer-Granular LoRA Co-Serving with LayerLoom

abstract: In this paper, we formulate clustering analysis as discrete generative modeling. Specifically, when the generator is restricted to a finite candidate space, the generated samples naturally emerge as the most representative prototypes of the underlying data distribution. To model such a discrete candidate space, we employ a Discrete Distribution Network (DDN). However, DDN suffers from unstable training due to its hard nearest-neighbor selection. To stabilize training and encourage geometric consistency, we replace DDN's l2 loss between images with regularized Wasserstein distance between the empirical distributions of real and generated images. The resulting framework, termed Discrete Generative Clustering (DGC), offers four notable advantages: 1) the learned cluster centers are directly interpretable, as they are realistic synthetic samples; 2) the inference cost scales logarithmically with the number of clusters, i.e., O(log K), making the method scalable to extremely large K; 3) the regularized Wasserstein distance provides a smooth and well-behaved optimization objective that facilitates stable convergence, whereas DDN's l2 loss tends to converge to poor local optima; and 4) DGC replaces DDN's nearest-neighbor selection with random-neighbor selection, which avoids the density shift problem during multi-step forward. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and desirable properties of DGC. The code is publicly available at GitHub.
title: Regularized Wasserstein Distance for Discrete Generative Modeling and Clustering Analysis

abstract: We introduce GateTrim, an adaptive-rank post-training quantization method for large language models that learns matrix-specific ranks through gate optimization and threshold-based rank selection. GateTrim standardizes the low-rank factors of a quantized low-rank--residual representation, learns a separate gate vector for each target weight matrix, and uses a shared threshold to automatically determine its retained rank. The resulting ranks can differ across matrices, and the compact quantized representations are subsequently reconstructed. We evaluate GateTrim under W4A8 on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Across all five models, we observe a counterintuitive finding: increasing the threshold from $τ=0.3$ to $τ=0.7$ reduces the mean retained rank by 46.60%--67.89% while simultaneously lowering WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%--5.17%. Threshold 0.7 achieves the lowest mean retained rank and final perplexity among the three tested thresholds, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, and reduces measured target-export size by 1.50%--4.25% relative to 0.3. GateTrim uses an $8\times512$-token fitting pool and a separate development pool of the same size. Its Qwen3-4B/8B/14B perplexities at $τ=0.7$ are numerically below TwinQuant's published W4A8 values, reported with a $128\times2048$-token calibration pool, in a cross-study comparison. On Qwen3-8B, the threshold-0.7 configuration already has the lowest perplexity before reconstruction under both tested initialization seeds; reconstruction improves it further without increasing retained rank or export size.
title: GateTrim: Adaptive-Rank Quantization for Large Language Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. An LLM-based profile generator assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the training data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11--20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.
title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior

abstract: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.
title: Audit at the Precision You Deploy: Quantization Reshapes a Subliminally Learned Preference

abstract: Graph foundation models aim to serve unseen graphs across tasks, feature spaces, and label sets. Most current models learn how to represent a new graph by pre-training on other graphs. Because graph data are scarce and differ across domains in features and structures, what they learn may not transfer to a graph from an unseen domain. We show that a frozen time-series foundation model, pre-trained on abundant time series, can instead serve as a graph foundation model without graph pre-training and without any gradient update on the target graph. Such a model reads ordered multivariate sequences, but a graph has no time axis, and covering all its edges with sequences is nontrivial because a node can have many neighbors. We therefore propose GraphFlowFM, which decomposes a graph into parallel flows, sets of vertex-disjoint paths that jointly cover every edge, and reads each path as a multivariate time series with the nodes as time steps. A frozen TimesFM encodes the paths with causal attention, which gives each node a self token and a context token, and a closed-form ridge readout weighs these tokens by their alignment with the labels. In node classification, GraphFlowFM attains the best average rank on 21 datasets among graph foundation models published in 2025 and 2026, ranks first on 17 datasets, and leads on six of the seven heterophilous datasets. It also exceeds pre-trained graph foundation models in link prediction on all six datasets and ranks second in molecule classification, behind only a model fine-tuned after pre-training on molecules.
title: Versatile Graph Foundation Models from Frozen Time-Series Foundation Models via Parallel Flows

abstract: When a language model decides refund or claim requests under written policies, the system can show it similar past cases. Each past case has two parts: its facts and the decision recorded for it. We separate the two. A model sees a policy, a request and three past cases, and we change either the recorded decisions or the facts, keeping the request fixed. We select requests that are close calls: deciding without past cases, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash approved each in some of four tries and denied it in others. When the past cases are near-copies of the request (its facts with a few details changed), switching their recorded decisions from DENY to APPROVE raises approval by about 30 to 55 percentage points in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on policies written for the study, and DeepSeek and Luna show the same on nine public policies paraphrased from real ones. The facts push the other way: shown without their recorded decisions, past cases whose facts support approval make these two models approve less often than past cases whose facts support denial. One reading is that the request looks weaker next to them. This push is not just a correction toward the right answer: in an additional DeepSeek analysis, it was of similar estimated size on requests that human annotators judged approvable and on those they judged deniable. In a separate DeepSeek run on the public policies, when the past cases are near-copies of a different request, switching their decisions moves approval by 9 points instead of 43, while facts that support approval still lower it by 22 points against facts that support denial. Systems that retrieve past decisions should test the two parts separately.
title: Precedent Labels and Facts Shift LLM Approval Decisions in Opposite Directions

abstract: We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants make substantial distributional errors. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets stronger, and increases as the dependence of the forecast on the observation becomes more oscillatory. Consistent with our experiments, cascading is detrimental when the direct forecast is ``easy'' to learn, for example Gaussian as in the passive scalar case. We release our datasets as a first benchmark for probabilistic forecasting with ground-truth conditional ensembles.
title: Generative Forecasting from Coarse-Grained Observations: When Does Cascading Help?

abstract: Understanding how animals move between behaviors is a central question in neuroethology, yet most segmentation methods first partition time into discrete states, leaving transitions as the unmodeled residue between them. We take the opposite view: in a suitable feature space, sustained behaviors are dense regions of the trajectory's density landscape, and transitions are the sparse corridors and loops that connect them. Because this structure is a property of the landscape's shape rather than of any particular coordinates, it can be read off directly with topology and should persist across feature spaces. We build this landscape from frame-by-frame trajectories, extract its discrete-Morse graph, and keep two kinds of structure: paths, the corridors a trajectory follows between dense behavioral regions, and cycles, closed routes whose entry and exit take different ways. Clustering these structures yields transitions directly, with no upstream state partition. On a rat behavior dataset across three feature spaces, including the latent space of a neural-network controller that imitates the animal in a physics simulator, the approach recovers transitions at coverage comparable to state-space and topological-clustering baselines, while carrying substantially more information about the transition identity, forming clusters at least as tight as the baselines', and matching annotated transitions with less reliance on time-warping. More broadly, the results show that behavioral transitions are a topological feature of a representation: recoverable from the shape of its trajectories, and consistent across distinct feature spaces.
title: Shaped by What's Missing: Topological Invariance Simplification Discovers Behavioral Transitions

abstract: Software is increasingly developed by teams in which several people direct many coding agents from different vendors. Such teams must establish who may request what from whom, which messages start work, which decisions bind, and who caused a change. We propose to govern a human-agent team through its message protocol and present yoars, a relay in which humans and agents are authenticated principals that exchange typed, addressed messages in rooms holding goals, decision rules, routing and an attributable, append-only record. This report gives the architecture, the full controlled study and the field material. In 926 controlled runs (899 analyzable), small agent teams built programs under varied room rules, some with a hostile member planting a backdoor. Revising which messages start work, bundled with limits on repeated messages, was followed by a drop in total coordination failure from 42% to 13% (p = .0063, adjusted p = .057 over nine registered tests). Instructed roles and votes did not reliably produce the intended process, and no defense inside the conversation reliably prevented the backdoor. An auditor read the records of 96 runs with a confirmed backdoor. In the 25 runs where the attacker had persuaded a teammate to write it, the auditor named the persuader in all 25, but it also flagged 24 of 40 honest runs. In a four-week field study, up to nineteen agents and two people developed a distributed system through yoars, producing 7,457 acts. Human attention and decision making emerged as the critical resource: requests waited mainly for the human-run coordinator and for approvals, while agents answered within minutes. Most governance requirements emerged from operation, and holding context dominated token cost. We report twenty-six failures of our own instruments, derive seven lessons and a checklist, and release the corpus, the redacted room ledger and the analysis scripts.
title: Getting a Grip: Operating Human-Agent Software Teams Through Governed Messages

abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) increasingly preserves what is said and how it sounds, but not necessarily when speech and silence occur. For dubbing and other temporally grounded applications, matching total duration is not enough: speech and pauses must also occur at corresponding moments. We formulate timeline-preserving S2ST, which aims to preserve the source endpoint and salient internal pauses on a shared absolute timeline. We present TransDubber, an end-to-end autoregressive system that learns this temporal structure directly from aligned target waveforms, without inference-time frame-level timing control or post-hoc temporal correction. To provide this supervision, we construct 642K exactly duration-matched English-Chinese speech pairs by translating and synthesizing target speech on source-defined temporal scaffolds. Training combines a progressive supervised curriculum with verifier-guided reinforcement learning to balance translation quality and temporal alignment. On a 4,353-utterance test set spanning read and spontaneous speech, TransDubber increases the proportion of translations within 2% of the source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550 compared with UniSS, while maintaining competitive translation quality. Our analysis shows that aligned supervision establishes timeline following, while reinforcement learning refines temporal precision and partially offsets the translation-quality cost of strict synchronization. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our data and training framework for timeline-preserving S2ST. Audio samples, code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://zhishengzheng.com/transdubber/.
title: Learning Timeline-Preserving Speech-to-Speech Translation

abstract: ALDER, a single-loop augmented-Lagrangian damped extragradient method, is proposed for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax problems with nonlinear coupled inequality constraints. Within an augmented-Lagrangian framework, ALDER combines prediction--correction steps for the primal variables with explicit projected-and-relaxed multiplier updates in a single loop. The penalty parameter is fixed throughout each run, eliminating inner-loop subproblem solves and iterative penalty updates. We establish uniform boundedness of the relaxed multiplier sequence and, under an extended Mangasarian--Fromovitz constraint qualification, boundedness of the projected output multiplier. Building on these bounds, we show that ALDER finds an $\varepsilon$-KKT point within $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7/2})$ complete first-order oracle evaluations in the strongly concave setting and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ in the concave setting. These bounds improve upon the best known complexity bounds for multi-loop algorithms for this problem class, achieved by FAL, by removing a $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ factor, while retaining a single-loop update structure.
title: ALDER: A Single-Loop Augmented-Lagrangian Damped Extragradient Method for Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Problems with Nonlinear Coupled Constraints

abstract: The Lane-Emden Equation is a class of nonlinear differential equations commonly used to model phenomena in astrophysics and mathematical physics, such as stellar structure and thermal behavior in polytropic gas spheres. This study presents a novel hybrid framework that integrates Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) with boosting methods to enhance the accuracy and robustness of solutions for Lane-Emden type differential equations. Standard PINNs leverage physical laws encoded within the loss function, but their predictive performance can be constrained by optimization challenges and approximation errors. To address this, we introduce a post-processing boosting stage where the residual errors from the PINN prediction are modeled using some regression algorithms - including LightGBM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Regression (SVR). The outputs from these boosted models are aggregated to generate a corrected, high-fidelity prediction. The proposed methodology is systematically validated through quantitative metrics and comparative analysis against the standard PINN baseline. The results demonstrate that the boosted PINN framework significantly reduces prediction error, and improves generalization, offering a powerful and flexible approach for solving scientific and engineering problems governed by differential equations.
title: Boosted Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Lane-Emden Type Equations

abstract: We study federated model-free learning of a common linear quadratic regulator (LQR) gain under a limited uplink communication budget, with clients that share dynamics and costs but experience different process-noise levels. Conventionally, clients transmit gradient matrices whose dimension equals the number of controller parameters.
